question: Under the constraints $x+2y\le12$, $3x+y\le15$, $x\ge0$ and $y\ge0$, consider the three proposed solutions $P(n,0)$, $Q(n-1,1)$ and $R(n-2,2)$, where $n$ is an integer with $n\ge2$. Determine the greatest value of $n$ for which all three are feasible solutions and verify that increasing $n$ by one produces an infeasible proposed solution.
explanation:
Verification for $P(n,0)$
The constraints give $n\le12$ and $3n\le15$, so $n\le5$. Thus $P$ can be feasible only when $n\le5$. Since this is already the strongest restriction obtained from $P$, any value larger than 5 cannot make all three points feasible.

Verification for the Remaining Proposed Solutions
For $Q(n-1,1)$, the first constraint gives $(n-1)+2\le12$, so $n\le11$, while the second gives $3(n-1)+1\le15$, so $3n-2\le15$ and $n\le\frac{17}{3}$. Since $n$ is an integer, this gives $n\le5$. For $R(n-2,2)$, the first constraint gives $(n-2)+4\le12$, so $n\le10$, while the second gives $3(n-2)+2\le15$, so $3n-4\le15$ and $n\le\frac{19}{3}$, giving $n\le6$ for integral $n$.

Combining these conditions with $n\ge2$, all three proposed points are feasible for integer values $2\le n\le5$. Hence the greatest possible value is $n=5$.

When $n$ is increased to 6, $P=(6,0)$ gives $3x+y=18>15$, so it violates a constraint and is infeasible. Also, $Q=(5,1)$ gives $3x+y=16>15$ and is infeasible.

Final Result
The greatest integer value for which all three proposed points are feasible is $n=5$; at $n=6$, at least one proposed point violates the constraints and becomes infeasible.

options.A: The greatest value is $n=6$; at $n=7$, only $R$ becomes infeasible
options.B: The greatest value is $n=4$; at $n=5$, $P$ becomes infeasible
options.C: The greatest value is $n=5$; at $n=6$, $P$ and $Q$ violate $3x+y\leq15$
options.D: The greatest value is $n=5$; all three points remain feasible at $n=6$
